questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy - SiO housing is very efficient in getting a accomadation

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Oslo is very small - It's not as important being close to campus, as you can very easily access the uniersity through public transport - Try to be as central as possible for more social possibilities

Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: All done through Erasmus+ - Courses can be found on the website and information of how to request is sent. If you miss the deadline, it's possible to contact the faculties to still be part of courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: All faculties were very helpful and reaching out to them was very easy and rewarding to do.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all the classes i wanted - 100% success

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You're not forced to only take forces from your own line of education - Search the catalouge of UiO to find intresesting courses, that are not specifically part of your own studies (Or at least research it).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was doing a individual research project for an academic group the university, as preparation for my master thesis. This provided me with incredibly high level insight into academia, and in many ways went above master level. To supplement this, I had advanced courses taught by nobel-prize winning teachers, whom taught what they had helped discover.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A little more relaxed, yet still firm. The definition of "Freedom under responsibility". As long as you take responsibility for your own learning and engage, you have a lot of freedom in the course structure.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FRM5020 – Pharmaceutical research project
BIOS5812 – Advanced Physiology and Nevrobiology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Any course thats within your interest, but I really recommend during a research project, if you are going on exchange for the acadmical purpose. It'll give a lot of insight into the process. If cultural or social aspiration is the main priority, I recommend taking courses, so that you learn other students during classes.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not much - Pretty much the same costs as denmark

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Alcohol and food is very expensive, but clothes, especially outdoor clothes, are cheaper then in Denmark

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UiO has a very good student fitness association, with a lot of student driven organisations

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The UiO SiO provides a platform for students to create and share their own student association, where you can search and apply to those, that peak your interest.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Anything that requires you to be a group,or do something together - Sports, boardgames, politics. This is the best way to meet other students outside of school.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Make use of the beautiful nature of Norway - Visit the mountains or spend time in the parks. During winter, use some of the winter sport oppertunities, which aren't possible in Denmark

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy - Danish and Norwegian culture is very similar.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to people - Like in Denmark, we are very closed off untill we actually talk to people, and then people are quick to open up slightly. And just be honest about trying to find new friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Crosswalks are less regulated by lights and more by trust in the other person - Many crosswalks don't have light regulation outside the center of Oslo, and there's not a sophisticated bike lane system like in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: the norwegian connections with nature, and their philosophy of "life to work", instead of the other way around.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Enjoy the ride - There will be up and downs, but ultimately make the short amount of time you're aboard be as enjoyable as possible.
2. Carpe diem/Seize the day - You're experiencing a new country, and things will be different. Embrace the differences, and use them to learn about your own culture and yourself.
3. Take your time - Adjusting to a new daily life an take a while, and it differs for each person. Allow yourself to be frustrated with the changes, without blaming yourself because "You should be adjusted by now". You're your own bets ally in the exchange, so don't become your own worst enemy.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Learn to prepare lunches from home - Food is expensive, and therefore cafeteria food will also be expensive from what you're used to.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning and experiencing a new culture, and broaden your horizon, both in terms of language, people and culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Missing the usual everyday life, you had gotten used to before leaving. You will experiene homesickness and missing your friends and family, which can be tough. However, getting through that and learning to appreciate what you are returning home to, is a great personal growth as well.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
